lesson_title: Why Builders Trust the Little Ruler, Not the Ratio
hook_text: That plan says 1 : 50. Photocopy it once and that number becomes a lie. The little printed ruler doesn't.
clip_script: A plan is just a house that has been shrunk until it fits on a page, and the scale is the honest label saying by how much. One to fifty means the drawing is fifty times smaller than the real thing — every centimetre on the paper is fifty centimetres of actual wall. Measure the bedroom: 9,0 centimetres. Times 50 is 450 centimetres, which is 4,50 metres. You just measured a room you have never stood in. Page to reality, multiply. Reality to page, divide. Now the part everyone loves asking about. Why do plans also carry a little printed ruler next to the ratio? Because a photocopier does not know about ratios. Shrink that page to 80 percent and one-to-fifty is suddenly false — one centimetre no longer means fifty. But the little printed ruler shrank too. It lives on the same page, so it squashes and stretches with the drawing, and it keeps telling the truth at any size. That is why the builder measures against the bar and treats the ratio as a label.
visual_style: A house folding down onto a sheet of paper, a ruler laid along a wall reading 9,0 cm then flipping to 4,50 m; then the page visibly shrinking in a photocopier while the printed bar scale shrinks with it and the '1 : 50' text cracks apart.
pacing: Brisk measuring demo, dramatic pause at the photocopier, calm confident close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and price a room's carpet, skirting and paving straight off the plan.
